newsitem.title: USA: Andrews offers to combine Toy Biz and Marvel.
newsitem.headline: Andrews offers to combine Toy Biz and Marvel.

text.p: Financier Ronald Perelman's Andrews Group offered Tuesday to combine the operations of Toy Biz Inc. and Marvel Entertainment Group in a $350 million deal that would allow Perelman to retain control of Marvel.
Toy Biz is licensed to make toys based on Marvel's comic characters, including X-Men, Spiderman and the Incredible Hulk.

The offer came as Marvel reported a third-quarter loss of $12.5 million and warned of continuing losses in the current quarter. Marvel said weak publishing and trading card sales have forced it to consider a restructuring and other actions, which could result in substantial 1996 year-end charges.

The Toy Biz deal will make Marvel a stronger operating company, according to John Kyle Cartwright, high-yield bond analyst at Wheat First Butcher Singer. "Marvel Entertainment will no longer be a bankruptcy candidate," he said.
An Andrews spokesman said the alternative to this deal might be a Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing for Marvel that would leave investors with nothing.
But Marvel's stock fell as the deal would involve issuing 410 million new Marvel shares, on top of slightly more than 100 million shares already outstanding.
Marvel fell $1.875 to $2.75 on the New York Stock Exchange in late trading. Toy Biz lost 12.5 cents to $17.625, also on the NYSE.
Perelman's holding companies already hold about 80.2 percent of Marvel's common stock. Perelman would maintain his stake in this deal, the Andrews spokesman said.

Andrews last month agreed to acquire about 67 percent of Toy Biz's class A common stock from Isaac Perlmutter and Avi Arad, an Andrews spokesman said. Marvel currently holds all of Toy Biz's Class B common stock.
The deal would let Perelman's companies that control Marvel walk away from nearly $900 million in debt in exchange for his $350 million investment in Toy Biz, said Cartwright.
Much of the debt, controlled by Perelman through various holding companies, is secured by Marvel common stock.

Marvel said separately that its loss, equal to 12 cents a share, in the third quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with profits of $19.6 million, or 19 cents a share, in the year-ago period. Revenues fell to $209.4 million from $269.0 million.

As a result of continuing trends in its businesses, Marvel expects to report a loss of 25 cents to 30 cents a share for its fourth quarter ending Dec. 31, and a loss of 52 cents to 57 cents for full-year 1996.

The estimated 1996 loss is expected to include operating losses of $10 million to $15 million from Marvel Comics Group publishing and licensing operations, and a loss of $10 million to $15 million from Fleer/SkyBox trading card operations, the company said. It also includes an operating profit from international operations.
